title: This ranking publishes a score with no sample size and no uncertainty, so no difference read off it can be called real
detects: A row from a public leaderboard whose scores carry no sample size, no standard error and no interval. The number is still the number; what cannot be done with it is the thing readers do with it constantly, which is compare two of them. Without a sample size there is no interval, and without an interval there is no way to tell a real gap between two models from the ordinary variation between two runs of the same model.
incident: Measured on the UGI Leaderboard's own published data file on 2026-10-05: 1,326 rows, 71 columns, and not one confidence interval, standard error or sample size among them. The leaderboard keeps its question set confidential, which is a sound choice that stops publishers training against the test, and the cost of it falls here: nobody outside the project can rerun it, so nobody can establish the variation either. A nearby project supplies the scale of the problem. Three configurations compared at 200 items looked like a clean ordering across a spread of 0.017, and then the same configuration run twice moved by 0.054, so the noise was three times the effect and all three arms were indistinguishable.
remedy: Treat the score as a position and not as a measurement. Do not quote a difference between two rows as a result, and do not quote a change in your own model's position across two test dates as an improvement or a regression. To make a claim about either, measure the property yourself on a set you can rerun, with the sample size and the interval recorded beside the figure. This checker's own `score` and `capability` commands do that, and so does any harness that reports a standard error.
false_positive: It fires on every row of every leaderboard shaped this way, which is accurate rather than noisy: the property it reports is a property of the publication and not of the model, and it is the same news for every row. That does make it unsuitable as a gate, and it is a note to a reader rather than something to fail a build on. It says nothing about whether the scores are any good: a carefully built benchmark with no published interval and a careless one with none are indistinguishable here, and this check does not attempt to tell them apart. If a leaderboard does publish a sample size in a column this adapter does not read, the fault is ours and the fix is to teach the adapter rather than to loosen the check.
